reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A rare glomerular disease defined by deposition of randomly arranged, non-branching fibrils in the mesangium and capillary walls that are larger than amyloid fibrils
Crucially, the fibrils do not stain with Congo red, which distinguishes it from amyloidosis
Immunostaining for DNAJB9 has emerged as a sensitive and specific tissue marker, greatly aiding diagnosis
Patients typically present with proteinuria (often nephrotic range), haematuria, hypertension, and chronic kidney impairment
Immunofluorescence usually shows polyclonal IgG (often IgG4) with C3 in a smudgy pattern along the capillary walls and mesangium
Associations reported include malignancy, hepatitis C infection, autoimmune disease, and, in some cases, monoclonal gammopathy, so a search for these is warranted
There is no established standard therapy; management combines supportive renal care with immunosuppression such as rituximab in selected patients
The disease may recur after kidney transplantation, though often with a slower course
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis is characterised by the accumulation of organised fibrillary material within the glomerulus. Unlike amyloid, these fibrils are Congo red negative and generally thicker (typically around 10-30 nm) and are composed largely of polyclonal immunoglobulin, complement, and the chaperone protein DNAJB9. The deposition disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier and incites mesangial expansion and capillary wall injury, producing proteinuria, haematuria, and progressive loss of function. The precise trigger is unknown, but the strong and specific presence of DNAJB9 suggests a central role for this protein in pathogenesis, and a subset of cases are linked to systemic conditions such as infection, autoimmunity, or malignancy.
additionalInvestigations: Kidney biopsy with Congo red staining (negative) and electron microscopy to identify fibrils
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains
Hepatitis C serology and autoimmune screen
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with declining kidney function
Evidence of an underlying malignancy or monoclonal disorder
reference.prognosis: Many patients progress to kidney failure over a few years, particularly those with heavy proteinuria and reduced function at presentation, though responses to immunosuppression occur in some and post-transplant recurrence tends to be indolent.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as amyloidosis without confirming a negative Congo red stain
Overlooking DNAJB9 staining, which can confirm the diagnosis
Failing to screen for associated infection, autoimmunity, or malignancy
Assuming a uniformly poor outcome and not considering targeted immunosuppression
